chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
title: Perez Prado's mambo versus his own arrangers
summary: Machito says the mambo was nothing new, Prado aimed at a mass American audience, and his arrangers were more advanced.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Okay. Macho, you are doing these Afro-Cuban recordings with Parker, Flip Phillips, for the Mercury label. The mambo is coming in. Perez Prado is recording these things out in California. What did you think when you first heard the mambo?

Well, to me it was nothing new. First of all because he had a lot of American influence in what he called mambo. You know, he is another talented fellow because I have recording with Cascarita. He was like - he want to create something, to create something, to manufacture something that was for the American public. He was shooting for two-hundred million people, he don't care about two-hundred million people, with good standard of living....
But what did it mean to you, that mambo?

To me, well, ahh with all due respect, because I am qualified to criticize anybody, we were more musical-advanced that what he had to produce because our arranger was to arranger and he was a well-inspired person, but you just can't I mean, compare Perez Prado with Chico O'Farrell, with Rene Hernandez, with Walter Fuller, with Edgar Samson ....
.... those people that was real pros.
